performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
intro: “Der Leiermann” is the twenty-fourth and last song of Schubert’s Winterreise, D. 911. An old man stands barefoot on the ice and turns his hurdy-gurdy, with an empty plate at his feet. The piano holds a bare fifth, and the traveller asks whether they might go on together.

sections.label: Intro · Piano drone fifth and repeated figure
sections.mNote: The piano plays a short repeated tune over a bare fifth.

sections.label: A · Old man, bare feet, empty plate
sections.mNote: The voice describes the old man beyond the village.

sections.label: B · Nobody listens, dogs growl; drone
sections.mNote: The singer returns over the same unchanging drone.

sections.label: B′ · Piano alone, four bars
sections.mNote: The voice rests; the piano repeats the short tune.

sections.label: C · The traveller addresses the old man
sections.mNote: The final line rises an octave over the drone.

sections.label: Coda · Piano postlude on opening figure
sections.mNote: The opening figure returns and ends on a minor chord.

cues.title: Introduction, open-fifth drone
cues.text: The piano holds a bare fifth in the bass. Above it, a short right-hand figure repeats, imitating the hurdy-gurdy’s wheel and drones. The singer enters after eight bars.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 1–8, open-fifth drone and recurring right-hand figure; original key A minor, transposed down a tone in this recording. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The hurdy-gurdy man on the ice
cues.text: The old man sways barefoot on the ice, and his small plate stays empty. Müller gave him frozen fingers, no audience and no earnings. The piano repeats its tune throughout.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Der Leiermann, first two stanzas: https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-leiermann-2. OpenScore Lieder, bars 17–26, second stanza and repetition of its last couplet: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Third stanza, bars 31–38
cues.text: “Keiner mag ihn hören, / Keiner sieht ihn an”: nobody cares to hear him, nobody looks at him. The dogs growl around the player. The same bare fifth continues under the voice.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Der Leiermann, third stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation of the German at https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-leiermann-2. OpenScore Lieder, bars 31–38: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Final stanza, bars 53–58
cues.text: “Wunderlicher Alter” (strange old man). The traveller addresses the hurdy-gurdy man directly for the first time and asks whether he may go with him and whether the hurdy-gurdy will accompany his songs. The voice rises an octave on the last question, in bars 56–57, and the piano holds its drone.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Der Leiermann, last stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation: https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-leiermann-2. OpenScore Lieder, bars 53–58, final question and octave rise in bars 56–57: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Piano postlude, bars 58–61
cues.text: The voice rests from bar 59. The piano repeats the opening figure and ends on a minor chord over the same drone. Müller’s poem ends with the traveller’s questions.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 58–61: opening figure returns, voice rests from bar 59, final minor chord. Müller’s poem ends with the traveller’s questions. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023; https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-leiermann-2
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The voice enters over the drone
transitions.from: Intro · Piano drone fifth and repeated figure
transitions.to: A · Old man, bare feet, empty plate
transitions.how: The voice enters after eight piano bars. The left hand keeps its open fifth, and the right hand’s turning figure fills the spaces between the vocal phrases. In Schubert’s original key of A minor the drone is A–E, with no third.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 1–16, original A-minor score; this performance is transposed down a tone. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023

transitions.title: Piano interlude into the third stanza
transitions.from: A · Old man, bare feet, empty plate
transitions.to: B · Nobody listens, dogs growl; drone
transitions.how: After the repeated lines about the empty plate, the piano plays four bars alone. At bar 31 the voice returns with the same melody and the words about nobody listening. The bass fifth continues across the join.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 27–38: piano interlude, third stanza from bar 31 and continuing drone. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023

transitions.title: Piano interlude after the fourth stanza
transitions.from: B · Nobody listens, dogs growl; drone
transitions.how: The fourth stanza ends, and the voice rests for four bars (bars 49–52). The piano repeats the interlude from bars 27–30. Its small right-hand figure turns above the open fifth while a short line moves beneath it in the left hand.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 49–52, matching the interlude at bars 27–30. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023

transitions.title: The singer addresses the old man
transitions.to: C · The traveller addresses the old man
transitions.how: The singer returns over the drone in bars 53–58 with repeated notes and speaks to the old man directly. The last line climbs an octave as he asks the old man to accompany his songs. The bass stays fixed beneath the rising voice.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 53–58; Müller, final stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023; https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-leiermann-2

transitions.title: Closing bars: the opening figure returns
transitions.from: C · The traveller addresses the old man
transitions.to: Coda · Piano postlude on opening figure
transitions.how: In bars 58–61, the piano begins its opening figure again while the singer holds his last note. The voice then stops, and the marking in bar 59 is piano. The same bass fifth continues as a drone beneath the final minor chord.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 58–61: returning figure, piano marking in bar 59, final minor chord above the drone. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5014023

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 24, Der Leiermann, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: Bars 1–61. Piano alone in bars 1–8, 27–30, 49–52 and 59–61. The singer holds the last note into bar 58 as the opening piano figure returns.

timeline.note: The piano begins with a bare fifth and a small turning figure.
The voice enters above the drone and describes the old man beyond the village.
The voice rests for four bars while the piano repeats its tune.
The singer returns with the lines about the empty audience and the growling dogs.
The piano repeats its four-bar interlude above the unchanged fifth.
The traveller addresses the old man; his last line rises an octave.
The voice holds its last note while the opening piano figure returns.
Three piano bars end the song on a minor chord above the drone.

voices: Voice (baritone; treble notation sounds one octave lower)

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: Utz measures this song at 3:10 against a mean of 3:41 and describes a clear slowing in its second part. No source consulted states the key of the transfer; the transposition from the first edition and the absolute pitch are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ER 276, and the Commons file name agrees. The Internet Archive text description of the disc reads “ER 376”, which the photograph does not support; the discrepancy is the uploader’s.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: BK 2969, take 1 (run-out “Bk 2969” with I); side No. 24 (label number 942922); reverse side: Die Nebensonnen (matrix CL 4401-1; pianist Lene Orthmann, 11 July 1928). Disc 12 of 12 of the set; 25 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (195.50 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (195.41 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
